cues.text: A Mind Fired Early with Love of Learning
Born in 1033 at Aosta, a town in the Italian Alps near the borders of France and Switzerland, Anselm showed an intense love of learning from earliest childhood.

He later recalled to his biographer Eadmer a vivid childhood memory of hearing his mother speak of God dwelling on high, ruling all things—an image that shaped his religious imagination from his earliest years.
Leaving home at twenty-three, Anselm traveled through France before settling at the Benedictine abbey of Bec in Normandy in 1059.
Drawn by the reputation of its prior, the celebrated theologian Lanfranc, Anselm saw his own extraordinary intellectual gifts begin to flourish under Lanfranc's guidance.
An Argument Born of Sleepless Nights
At Bec, where Anselm eventually succeeded Lanfranc as prior and then abbot, he composed the philosophical works on which much of his lasting fame rests.
Above all, these included the Proslogion , containing his celebrated ontological argument for the existence of God.

It reasons from God's very definition as "that than which nothing greater can be thought" to the conclusion that such a being must, by the force of that definition alone, exist in reality and not merely in the mind.
Eadmer records that Anselm became so consumed by working out this argument that, for days, he could think of nothing else.
At one point, he even neglected food until the insight finally came to him—a piece of reasoning philosophers still actively debate today.
The argument, first conceived by a monk in the depths of prayerful concentration nearly a thousand years ago, is still actively debated today.
Faith Seeking Understanding

Anselm's guiding theological principle, fides quaerens intellectum — "faith seeking understanding" — insisted that genuine faith, far from being threatened by rigorous reasoning, actively seeks deeper understanding of truths it already believes.
This conviction made Anselm one of the founding figures of the intellectual movement later ages would call Scholasticism .
It was the disciplined marriage of faith and philosophical reason that would flower fully in the great university theology of the following two centuries.
A Reluctant Archbishop
Anselm's reputation for holiness and learning drew him, much against his own preference for quiet monastic scholarship, to the archbishopric of Canterbury in 1093.
He accepted the position only with genuine reluctance, aware that it would draw him directly into fierce political conflicts convulsing the English Church.
These conflicts concerned who held ultimate authority over bishops and Church property: the pope, or the king.
Exiled Twice for the Church's Freedom
Anselm's episcopate was marked by open, sustained conflict with two successive English kings, William Rufus and Henry I.
Both sought to control episcopal appointments and Church revenues for their own political and financial advantage—a struggle known to history as the Investiture Controversy.

Rather than compromise the Church's spiritual independence from royal control, Anselm chose exile from England twice, spending years abroad in voluntary displacement rather than surrender what he judged to be a matter of genuine principle.
Legacy

Anselm died at Canterbury on 21 April 1109, having finally secured, shortly before his death, a working resolution to the investiture dispute that preserved meaningful Church independence from royal control.
Declared a Doctor of the Church in 1720, Anselm remains one of the towering intellectual figures of medieval Christianity.
He was a monk whose sleepless nights wrestling with a single philosophical argument helped found an entire tradition of rigorous Christian reasoning.

His willingness to endure repeated exile rather than compromise the Church's freedom showed that the same mind capable of the subtlest philosophical argument could also hold, with equal firmness, to a simple and costly principle of conscience.
Nine centuries later, philosophers who have never opened a page of his theology still argue over the proof he first worked out, half-starved, in a Norman cloister.
